name: Tomas Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what happens on a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the dough divider and first prover on nights at a large bread bakery. My vocational certificate taught me the machine basics, and years on the line taught me to weigh the first pieces before a whole rack goes wrong. I am an experienced operator, but this plant pays below the usual rate.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Ana is a teaching assistant; we have two school-age children, a mortgage and only about three weeks saved. There are few similar plants nearby. I use an AI chat tool now and then for household letters, but I want a full safe run before trusting a new work control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the bakery crew AI might make a neat dough report, but the divider still has to give each loaf the right weight. I use an AI chat tool now and then for letters at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the divider after years on nights and hold a vocational certificate, but the wage is below most operators. Ana’s teaching-assistant pay is small, and our two children, mortgage and three weeks saved keep the boiler repair waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking dough weights at the first prover and take paid extra hours when the bakery offers them. If a full month leaves anything after mortgage and food, I would put a fresh amount from wages toward the boiler repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the bills already. A small AI plateau does not make a cold house cheaper to fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check the divider?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I weigh the first six pieces and look for one that sticks to the knife. If the average is low, I call the lead before the trays reach the prover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How soon could the boiler be repaired?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only when actual pay leaves enough for a safe repair. Ana and I will get a quote first; we cannot count unoffered overtime as cash.

say: I would tell the **bakery crew** dough weight still needs checking.
I would keep **occasional AI use** to household letters.
think: My **low night wage** and Ana’s smaller pay leave little spare.
The **mortgage and boiler** strain a three-week reserve.
do: Weigh **first dough pieces** and call the lead on divider drift.
Take **paid extra hours** only if the bakery offers them.
Put **fresh surplus pay** toward the boiler after bills.
feel: **Anxious** about baseline household costs, even with small AI change.
S0.quote: A small AI plateau does not make a cold house cheaper to fix.
fieldNote: Tomas’s experienced work and **vocational certificate** coexist with lower-than-usual pay.
His boiler plan depends on **actual new wages** and a repair quote from a qualified tradesperson, not assumed overtime.

steps.text: Keep weighing divider output and calling lead on drift
Set aside new surplus wages for quoted boiler repair

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell management faster orders are useful if the dough still gets its full proving time. I would ask the union representative to bring paid setup hours into the next rota discussion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could tighten the schedule before robots touch dough, and the plant might squeeze paid cleaning between batches. If my own night hours shrink, Ana’s school wage would not cover our mortgage; our three-week reserve would vanish quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record paid cleaning time across four night runs and bring it to the union meeting. If a new AI temperature alert works through a full week and the bakery offers paid practice on a stopped divider, I would learn it; after two shorter rosters we would delay the boiler’s nonurgent work and look at posted local food-line jobs that cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about paid time, though I can see a way to check a useful alert. I have changed machines before. I want a colleague to show me the new AI dough-temperature alert before I use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove the alert useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would catch dough temperature drifting before the first six pieces go light. I would compare its warnings with our actual scale records for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which boiler work could wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The noisy casing could wait, but any unsafe fault would have to be fixed. I would ask the repairer to separate those costs before changing the booking.

say: I would insist on **paid cleaning time** in faster bakery schedules.
I would take **night-run records** to the union representative.
think: My **own hours** could shrink before physical robots reach the divider.
Ana’s **school wage** and our thin reserve cannot carry the mortgage alone.
do: Record **four paid cleanings** and present the minutes at a union meeting.
Learn the **new AI alert** only after a proven week and offered paid stopped-line practice.
Check **local food-line vacancies** at bill-covering pay after two reduced rosters, delaying only nonurgent boiler casing.
feel: **Anxious** about income, while willing to learn a proven alert.
S1.quote: I want a colleague to show me the new AI dough-temperature alert before I use it.
fieldNote: His steady approach needs **one week of evidence** and offered paid practice before new controls.
The spending delay concerns **nonurgent casing**, never an unsafe boiler fault.

steps.text: Bring four paid night-cleaning records to union meeting
Learn AI temperature alert if offered paid stopped-line practice after proven week
Delay only nonurgent boiler casing after two reduced rosters
Check posted local food-line jobs at bill-covering pay after two reduced rosters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the night crew thinking AI reaches orders in 2028 when I am forty five, and capable hands-on robots reach dividing around 2031 when I am forty eight. I would ask who signs off bread weights if fewer of us stand at the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most divider tending hours to disappear once robots clear jams and adjust dough. Ana’s pay will not meet the mortgage and our three-week reserve cannot bridge months without mine; I lie awake hearing the boiler knock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel the children’s paid weekend outing and get the bakery’s written staffing plan. If my hours end, I would apply to a posted reachable food-production job only if the wage covers our bills and paid safe instruction is offered; if no opening exists, I would ask the lender about a temporary payment plan before missing a mortgage instalment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by a likely big wage loss. A course poster will not make our next payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you operate a robot during a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request a paid supervised demonstration behind a tested guard. I would touch controls only with an offered paid place and a qualified fitter showing the stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show her the staffing plan and our bills before promising a new job. We would keep essential boiler safety work and cut optional costs first.

say: I would say **2028 ordering AI** precedes capable divider robots around 2031.
I would ask for a **bread-weight sign-off** before staff are cut.
think: I expect **most tending hours** to go if robots clear jams.
Ana’s wage and **three-week savings** cannot cover a long mortgage gap.
do: Cancel the **paid weekend outing** and request written staffing dates.
Apply after **lost hours** only for posted reachable bill-covering work with paid safe instruction.
Ask the **lender** about a possible temporary plan if no adequate job appears.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless household worry.
S2.quote: A course poster will not make our next payment.
fieldNote: He expects **large hours loss** and describes sleepless worry, grounding alarm in household income.
Robot practice needs an **offered place** with paid time, while a lender plan is only a request.

steps.text: Cancel paid weekend outing and request written staffing plan
Apply after lost hours to posted reachable bill-covering job with paid safe instruction
Ask lender for possible temporary mortgage plan if no adequate job appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I am forty eight, with capable bakery robots around 2034 when I am fifty one. Five years gives the plant time to teach maintenance while we still earn wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might still need the divider pay at fifty one, but a real maintenance post could offer a better route. I would not leave this wage for an unpaid course or a certificate with no job behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the night shift and ask the bakery for a fully funded practical maintenance course with paid workshop days and an offered place. If a posted nearby role pays enough for our mortgage and includes written safe isolation duties, I would enrol; after qualifying I would apply for that role and put any new surplus wages into the boiler fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the divider work, but the extra time lets me check actual terms. I can learn a bearing repair beside a fitter if the study day is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What practical work would the course need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would isolate a stopped divider with a qualified fitter and replace a worn bearing before restart. A video of the repair would not qualify me to do it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is not offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the paid night line and ask the union to seek a funded place. I cannot buy a private course while our boiler still needs attention.

say: I would ask for **paid maintenance teaching** before 2034 bakery robots spread.
I would separate **2031 thinking AI** from physical line work.
think: The **mortgage** may still need divider wages at fifty one.
A **maintenance certificate** helps only with a posted adequate local role.
do: Keep the **paid night shift** while seeking a funded workshop place.
Enrol in **funded paid-time maintenance training** only with offered practice and a posted bill-covering safe role.
Apply after **qualifying** for that local role; save new surplus pay for the boiler.
feel: **Anxious**, with a practical route only if real offers appear.
S3.quote: I can learn a bearing repair beside a fitter if the study day is paid.
fieldNote: Tomas accepts **hands-on maintenance training** after proven paid terms, fitting his steady adaptability.
Enrolment and later application preserve **material conditions** on place, funding, paid days, posting, wage and safe isolation.

steps.text: Keep paid divider shift while training terms are checked
Enrol in funded paid maintenance course if offered place and posted bill-covering safe job exist
Apply after qualifying for posted local maintenance role with safe isolation duties

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union thinking AI comes in 2036 when I am fifty three, with capable divider robots around 2039 when I am fifty six. Thirteen years before physical robots should buy us paid practical training, not unpaid promises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children may be grown by then, but I cannot assume the mortgage is gone or Ana’s wage has risen. The boiler and three-week reserve matter now, and I may still need bakery work at fifty six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep weighing dough on paid nights and bring the cleaning-time records to the union. In the first year after 2036, if still employed, I would compare actual hours with posted local maintenance or production jobs; after two reduced rosters I would apply only where the wage covers our bills and safe training is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money today, uneasy about the distant robot. I would rather keep a real night wage than plan on a pension nobody has priced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a long course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not from three weeks of savings. If a funded paid practical place and a real local job at adequate pay open, I would consider the course after seeing it work for a colleague.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you work until 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if safe paid work remains and our household still needs wages. I cannot promise a bakery job or my health thirteen years out.

say: I would ask for **paid practical training** before 2039 bakery robots.
I would keep **2036 thinking AI** separate from physical work.
think: The **mortgage and boiler** remain costs today.
I may still need **safe paid bakery work** at fifty six.
do: Keep **paid night shifts** while employed and safe.
Apply after **two reduced post-2036 rosters** only to posted bill-covering work with paid safe training.
feel: **Anxious** about present bills and uneasy about later robots.
S4.quote: I would rather keep a real night wage than plan on a pension nobody has priced.
fieldNote: His **baseline cash pressure** keeps the ten-year picture from feeling secure.
He distinguishes **2026 paid shifts** from future work that depends on actual rosters, postings, wages and safety.

steps.text: Keep weighing dough on paid night shifts while employed and safe
Bring paid night-cleaning records to union
Apply after two reduced rosters to posted bill-covering local job with paid safe training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable bakery robots could take most of my paid divider hours around 2031 while our mortgage continues. Written staffing dates, funded paid practical training and a posted reachable job at bill-covering pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the first six pieces when a robot adjusts dough by itself. The mortgage needs a real night wage while I learn another machine.

headlineQuote: The mortgage needs a real night wage while I learn another machine.
portrait: **Tomas**, 43, is an experienced bakery divider operator with a vocational certificate and below-usual pay.
His **teaching-assistant wife**, two children, mortgage, three-week reserve and few nearby plants leave little room for lost shifts.
He uses AI **occasionally** at home and learns work controls after a proven safe run and offered paid practice.
His **baseline worry** persists under a plateau; expected major divider-hour loss makes the fast case alarming.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove Tomas’s divider hours around 2031 before his household builds a reserve.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, funded paid practical training and posted reachable jobs with enough wage would help.
